title: Diffusion: learning to remove noise
summary: A fixed forward process slowly turns data into Gaussian noise. Because Gaussians compose, any noise level can be reached in one jump: x_t = √ᾱ_t·x_0 + √(1−ᾱ_t)·ε. A network is trained by plain regression to predict the added noise ε, and generation runs the process backwards from pure noise, removing a little predicted noise at each step. The predicted noise points away from likely data, which links diffusion to score matching.
llm_link: Text-to-image models condition the denoiser on a text encoder's embeddings, so a language model's representation of your prompt steers every denoising step. Unlike an LLM, which writes one token after another, a diffusion model refines the whole output a little at each step.
key_ideas: Forward process (fixed): q(x_t | x_{t−1}) = N(√(1−β_t)·x_{t−1}, β_t·I). DDPM (Ho, Jain & Abbeel, 2020) used T = 1000 and β rising linearly from 10⁻⁴ to 0.02. The idea goes back to Sohl-Dickstein et al. (2015).
Closed form: ᾱ_t = Π_{s≤t}(1 − β_s) and x_t = √ᾱ_t·x_0 + √(1−ᾱ_t)·ε, ε ~ N(0, I).
Training: sample x_0, t, ε; build x_t in one jump; minimise ‖ε − ε_θ(x_t, t)‖² (the 'simplified' objective).
Sampling: start at x_T ~ N(0, I); each step removes a scaled predicted noise, rescales and adds a little fresh noise. Later samplers (e.g. DDIM) use far fewer steps.
The noise prediction is proportional to minus the score ∇ log p(x_t): the connection to score matching (Song & Ermon, 2019).
Conditioning on text plus classifier-free guidance controls the output; Dhariwal & Nichol (2021) reported diffusion beating GANs on image benchmarks.

quiz.q: Predict the result: ᾱ_t = 0.64, the clean value x_0 = 1.0 and the noise sample ε = 0.5. What is x_t = √ᾱ_t·x_0 + √(1−ᾱ_t)·ε?
What does the DDPM network learn to predict in the simplified objective?
options: The noise ε that was added to make x_t
quiz.explain: The target is ε, scored with squared error. Knowing ε and x_t you can also recover an estimate of x_0.

quiz.q: Why does the closed form x_t = √ᾱ_t·x_0 + √(1−ᾱ_t)·ε make training cheap?
options: It removes the need for a network
Any noise level can be sampled in one step, so you never simulate the whole chain during training
quiz.explain: Each training example picks a random t and builds x_t directly, so one network evaluation per example is enough.

quiz.q: Which part of a diffusion model is learned?
quiz.explain: The forward process is a fixed recipe; only the reverse (denoising) network has parameters.

quiz.q: In a text-to-image diffusion model, where does the language understanding come in?
options: The noise schedule is chosen by an LLM
The denoiser is conditioned on embeddings of the prompt from a text encoder at every step
The image is converted to tokens and generated left to right
quiz.explain: The text embedding is an extra input to ε_θ, and classifier-free guidance strengthens its effect.

problems.title: The noise schedule (NumPy)
problems.prompt:
Write alpha_bar(T, beta_start=1e-4, beta_end=0.02): make T betas spaced linearly from beta_start to beta_end, then return the running product of 1 − beta (an array of length T).

Then look at how much of the signal survives: sqrt(alpha_bar) is the weight on the clean image at each step.

ab = alpha_bar(1000)
ab[0]    # 0.9999
ab[-1]   # about 4e-05: almost pure noise

tests.name: length and first value
tests.code:
ab = alpha_bar(1000)
assert ab is not None, 'alpha_bar returned None'
assert len(ab) == 1000, f'expected 1000 values, got {len(ab)}'
assert abs(ab[0] - 0.9999) < 1e-12, f'the first value is 1 - 1e-4 = 0.9999, got {ab[0]}'

tests.name: ends near zero
tests.code:
ab = alpha_bar(1000)
assert abs(ab[-1] - 4.0358e-05) < 1e-7, f'after 1000 steps about 4e-5 of the signal variance remains, got {ab[-1]:.3e}. Use a product (np.cumprod), not a sum.'

tests.name: strictly decreasing
tests.code:
import numpy as np
ab = alpha_bar(50)
assert np.all(np.diff(ab) < 0), 'each step removes a bit more signal, so alpha_bar must decrease'

tests.name: custom schedule
tests.code:
import numpy as np
ab = alpha_bar(3, 0.1, 0.3)
assert np.allclose(ab, [0.9, 0.9 * 0.8, 0.9 * 0.8 * 0.7]), f'betas 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 give [0.9, 0.72, 0.504], got {ab}'

problems.title: Jump to any noise level
problems.prompt:
Write q_sample(x0, t, ab, eps) = sqrt(ab[t]) * x0 + sqrt(1 − ab[t]) * eps, where ab is the array from the previous problem (included below). The noise eps is passed in so tests are deterministic.

q_sample(np.array([1.0]), 0, np.array([0.64]), np.array([0.5]))   # array([1.1])

The last test checks a nice property: if the data has variance 1, so does every x_t. That is what the shrinking factor is for.

tests.name: worked example
tests.code:
import numpy as np
out = q_sample(np.array([1.0]), 0, np.array([0.64]), np.array([0.5]))
assert out is not None, 'q_sample returned None'
assert np.allclose(out, [1.1]), f'expected 0.8*1 + 0.6*0.5 = 1.1, got {out}. Use square roots of ab and of 1 - ab.'

tests.name: early steps keep the data
tests.code:
import numpy as np
ab = alpha_bar(1000); x0 = np.array([2.0, -1.0])
out = q_sample(x0, 0, ab, np.array([1.0, 1.0]))
assert np.allclose(out, x0, atol=0.02), f'at t = 0 almost no noise has been added, got {out}'

tests.name: late steps are almost pure noise
tests.code:
import numpy as np
ab = alpha_bar(1000); eps = np.array([0.3, -0.8])
out = q_sample(np.array([5.0, 5.0]), 999, ab, eps)
assert np.allclose(out, eps, atol=0.05), f'at the last step x_t should be essentially the noise, got {out}'

tests.name: variance stays 1
tests.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); ab = alpha_bar(1000)
x0 = rng.standard_normal(50000); eps = rng.standard_normal(50000)
v = q_sample(x0, 500, ab, eps).var()
assert abs(v - 1) < 0.03, f'unit-variance data should stay unit-variance at every step, got {v:.3f}'

hints: a = ab[t] is a single number.
return np.sqrt(a) * x0 + np.sqrt(1 - a) * eps

problems.title: A 1-D denoiser by least squares
problems.prompt:
Train the smallest possible noise predictor. The data are numbers drawn from N(2, 0.5²). At one fixed noise level (ᾱ = 0.5) make noisy samples x_t and the noise eps that made them, then fit a straight line eps_hat = a·x_t + b by least squares, exactly the regression a diffusion network does, with a line instead of a network.

Write fit_denoiser(xt, eps) returning (a, b) (use np.polyfit(xt, eps, 1), which returns [slope, intercept]).

For Gaussian data the best predictor really is a line, and the test compares your slope with the exact one: a* = √(1−ᾱ) / (ᾱ·s² + 1 − ᾱ) with s = 0.5.

    x0 = 2 + 0.5 * rng.standard_normal(n)
    eps = rng.standard_normal(n)
    xt = np.sqrt(ab) * x0 + np.sqrt(1 - ab) * eps
    return xt, eps

tests.name: slope matches theory
tests.code:
import numpy as np
xt, eps = make_data()
out = fit_denoiser(xt, eps)
assert out is not None, 'fit_denoiser returned None'
a, b = out
ab, s = 0.5, 0.5
astar = np.sqrt(1 - ab) / (ab * s**2 + 1 - ab)
assert abs(a - astar) < 0.02, f'expected slope near {astar:.3f}, got {a:.3f}. Fit eps as a function of xt (x first, y second in polyfit).'

tests.name: beats predicting zero
tests.code:
import numpy as np
xt, eps = make_data(seed=1)
a, b = fit_denoiser(xt, eps)
mse = np.mean((eps - (a * xt + b)) ** 2)
assert mse < 0.5 * np.mean(eps ** 2), f'the fitted line should remove well over half of the noise error, got MSE {mse:.3f} vs {np.mean(eps**2):.3f} for always guessing 0'

tests.name: denoised estimate of x0
tests.code:
import numpy as np
xt, eps = make_data(seed=2)
a, b = fit_denoiser(xt, eps)
ab = 0.5
x0_hat = (xt - np.sqrt(1 - ab) * (a * xt + b)) / np.sqrt(ab)
assert abs(x0_hat.mean() - 2) < 0.05, f'removing the predicted noise should recover data centred at 2, got mean {x0_hat.mean():.3f}'

hints: np.polyfit(x, y, 1) fits y ≈ slope·x + intercept. Here x is xt and y is eps.
a, b = np.polyfit(xt, eps, 1); return a, b
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def make_data(n=20000, ab=0.5, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    x0 = 2 + 0.5 * rng.standard_normal(n)
    eps = rng.standard_normal(n)
    xt = np.sqrt(ab) * x0 + np.sqrt(1 - ab) * eps
    return xt, eps

def fit_denoiser(xt, eps):
    a, b = np.polyfit(xt, eps, 1)
    return a, b
